passage: I'm Nazia. Looking back at last year, I can see how chaotic things were with Tanvir. When he held my hand at the college fest, I felt warm for about a minute, then my throat closed and I snatched my hand back and said something cruel about his shirt. Two days later I missed him so badly I rang him at midnight, crying. Then I got angry that he picked up. It made no sense, even to me. What's helping now: a friendship with Sheetal from my hostel that stays boring and steady, same lunch table every day, and my Tuesday sessions with the campus counsellor. Tanvir and I are just friends for now. Somehow that feels safer, and I don't hate it.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir hold Nazia's hand?
qa.a: He held Nazia's hand at the college fest.

qa.q: What did Nazia feel when Tanvir held hands at the fest, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nazia felt warm for a moment and then afraid; Nazia's throat closed, the hand was snatched back, and a cruel remark followed.

qa.q: What is helping Nazia change the pattern?
qa.a: A steady friendship with Sheetal and Tuesday sessions with the campus counsellor give Nazia calm, reliable connections to practise with.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have felt when he answered the midnight call and Nazia got angry?
qa.a: He probably felt confused and hurt, since he picked up to help and was blamed for it.

grounding: A young adult describes longing for love yet feeling danger when it comes close, and how steady friendship and a counsellor are helping.

passage:
Mentor's note, Anirban, first-year engineering hostel.
Divyansh, 19, came to our fortnightly chat looking wrecked. He had started seeing someone, and within a week he'd gone from texting her all night to telling her never to contact him again. Then he wrote her a long apology at three in the morning. "I want someone so badly," he said, "and then it feels like danger." He talked about his childhood home being loud and frightening at times, and about missing his late Dadi, the one calm person there. I didn't try to fix it. I asked if he'd see the campus counsellor; he agreed, and we booked it together. I also asked him to join the Sunday cricket group. Same faces every week.

qa.q: Which group did Anirban ask Divyansh to join?
qa.a: The Sunday cricket group, with the same faces every week.

qa.q: What does Divyansh mean when he says closeness "feels like danger"?
qa.a: He longs to be close but feels afraid when it comes near, perhaps because home was loud and frightening at times.

qa.q: What choice did Anirban make instead of trying to fix things?
qa.a: Anirban listened, then helped him book the campus counsellor together and suggested a steady weekly group.

qa.q: How might the person Divyansh was seeing have felt during that week?
qa.a: She was likely confused and unsettled, being texted all night, then told never to call, then sent an apology.

grounding: A mentor notes a young man whose longing and fear make love chaotic, and links him with a counsellor and a steady group.

passage: When Karthik texted, "I think I'm falling for you," Uma read it on the metro and felt two things at once: a rush of warmth, and the urge to throw the phone out of the window. By evening she had picked a fight over nothing and told him he was too needy; at midnight she sent a long message begging him not to go. Her flatmate Himani found her on the kitchen floor, crying. "I want this so much, and it feels like danger," Uma said. Himani didn't lecture. She made instant noodles, sat with her, and reminded her of the counsellor at the college wellness centre. "You liked her. Book it tomorrow. I'll walk you there." Uma nodded into her shoulder.

qa.q: Where did Uma read Karthik's text?
qa.a: On the metro.

qa.q: What two feelings did Uma have when she read the text?
qa.a: A rush of warmth and a sense of danger, wanting love yet scared of it coming close.

qa.q: How is Himani helping Uma build steadier support?
qa.a: By staying with her calmly and encouraging her to book the counsellor, offering to walk her there.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel after the fight and then the midnight message?
qa.a: Karthik is probably confused and hurt, being pushed away and then begged to stay on the same day.

grounding: Shows a young adult who longs for love but feels danger when it comes close, supported by a steady friend and a counsellor.

passage:
"You cancelled on her again?" Siddharth dropped onto Chinmay's hostel bed.
"She said she loves me, Sid. Out loud. In front of her friends."
"And that's bad?"
"No! It's all I've ever wanted." Chinmay pulled his knees up. "Then my chest went tight, like something terrible was coming. So I said I had a lab."
"You don't have labs on Sundays."
"I know." A long pause. "Last time I did this, I vanished for a week, then turned up at her door at midnight with flowers. She called it whiplash."
"We've played badminton every Wednesday for two years. I've never vanished on you, and you've never vanished on me."
"Because you're safe."
"So practise with safe people. And go back to that counsellor from first year."
"Will you come with me to book?"
"Wednesday. After badminton."

qa.q: What excuse did Chinmay give for cancelling?
qa.a: He said he had a lab.

qa.q: What did Chinmay feel when she said she loved him?
qa.a: He felt longing and joy, then a tight chest and dread, as if something terrible was coming.

qa.q: What steps does Siddharth suggest?
qa.a: Practising closeness with safe people and going back to the counsellor, with Siddharth coming along to book.

qa.q: What is it like for the girlfriend when Chinmay vanishes and then appears at midnight?
qa.a: She experiences it as whiplash, confused by the swing from distance to intensity.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who wants love deeply but panics when it comes near, and turns to a steady friend and a counsellor.

passage: The day Tenzin said he'd move to Pune for me, I went cold all over. I'd dreamt of someone choosing me like that since I was small. My father came and went so often that I learned not to watch the door. So when it finally happened, I said, "Don't you dare," and didn't speak to him for four days. Then I missed him so badly I couldn't breathe, and called at two in the morning saying sorry, sorry. I'm Dolma, twenty-two. I've started seeing a therapist every other Thursday. And I have two friends from the hostel I've kept for five years, which is its own small miracle. I'm learning love doesn't always come with a door slamming.

qa.q: How often does Dolma see a therapist?
qa.a: Every other Thursday.

qa.q: What did Dolma feel when Tenzin offered to move?
qa.a: Dolma felt a cold fear alongside a long-held longing, because being chosen felt dangerous after a father who came and went.

qa.q: What is helping Dolma change the pattern?
qa.a: Regular sessions with a therapist and steady friendships kept for five years.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt during the four days of silence?
qa.a: Tenzin was probably hurt and confused, having offered a big commitment and met silence.

grounding: Shows a young adult longing for love yet feeling danger when it arrives, starting to change through a therapist and steady friends.

passage:
College counsellor's note, Jyoti, second year, after our eighth session.
Jyoti came in angry today. "He was lovely, so I ended it before he could hurt me." Then, a minute later, she was crying for the relationship.
She keeps an old photo of herself at seven on her phone, from the year before her parents' separation, and says she misses "that girl who wasn't scared".
What I have noticed: she has come to every session on time, even the hard ones. She told me that trusting a routine felt "strange but calm". She mentioned her friend Jasleen, who texts her every Sunday and doesn't disappear when Jyoti goes quiet.
What we did next: we agreed that before ending anything, she will wait a day and talk it through here or with Jasleen. She also joined Jasleen's Sunday cooking group, low pressure and steady. We continue weekly.

qa.q: How often does Jasleen text Jyoti?
qa.a: Every Sunday.

qa.q: What did Jyoti feel about ending the relationship?
qa.a: She felt angry and afraid of being hurt, then sad and grieving for it a minute later.

qa.q: What steps might help Jyoti change the pattern over time?
qa.a: Waiting a day and talking it through before ending things, and building steady connections like weekly sessions and Jasleen's Sunday cooking group.

qa.q: How might Jasleen's steady Sunday texts affect Jyoti?
qa.a: They show Jyoti that someone can stay close without disappearing, which may slowly make closeness feel less dangerous.

grounding: Shows a counsellor noting a young adult who longs for love but ends it when it comes near, and who is building steady friendships and a reliable helper.
